notes.front: In Azure Pipelines, what is an agent?
notes.back: Computing infrastructure with the agent software installed, which runs one pipeline job at a time.
notes.explanation: You need at least one agent to build or deploy with Azure Pipelines, and more as the team grows.
notes.example: Like a GitHub Actions runner, but it picks up Azure Pipelines jobs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Azure Pipelines agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You need at least one agent to build your code or deploy your software by using Azure Pipelines. As your code base and team grow, you need multiple agents. When your pipeline runs, the system begins one or more jobs. An agent is computing infrastructure with installed agent software that runs one job at a time.

notes.front: What is an agent pool?
notes.back: A named group of agents that you register agents into and that pipelines pick agents from.
notes.explanation: A pipeline names a pool; with no pool set, a `YAML` pipeline uses the Azure Pipelines pool of Microsoft-hosted agents.
notes.example: Like a taxi rank: you ask the rank for a car, not a particular driver.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Communication with Azure Pipelines” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The user registers an agent with Azure Pipelines or Azure DevOps Server by adding it to an agent pool.

notes.front: What is a Microsoft-hosted agent?
notes.back: An Azure Pipelines agent hosted and managed by Microsoft, available in Azure DevOps Services.
notes.explanation: Microsoft runs the machines, so you only choose an image.
notes.example: Like a hire car handed over clean each time, instead of a car you own and service.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Azure Pipelines agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | [Microsoft-hosted agents](#microsoft-hosted-agents) | Agents hosted and managed by Microsoft. | Azure DevOps Services |

notes.front: What are GitHub-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines?
notes.back: Higher-performance Microsoft-managed agents on GitHub-hosted infrastructure, billed per minute of use.
notes.explanation: Microsoft-hosted agents, by contrast, use a concurrency-based pool.
notes.example: Like a Microsoft-hosted agent on a pay-per-minute meter with a bigger engine.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “GitHub-hosted agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: GitHub-hosted agents provide higher performance virtual machines for Azure Pipelines with pay-as-you-go (PAYG) billing. Unlike the Microsoft-hosted agents that use a concurrency-based pool, GitHub-hosted agents bill per minute of usage and offer more powerful machine configurations.

notes.front: What is a self-hosted agent?
notes.back: An agent that you set up and manage yourself to run jobs, in Azure Pipelines or Azure DevOps Server.
notes.explanation: You control the software installed on it, and its caches and configuration persist between runs.
notes.example: Like keeping your own work van, fitted out with your tools, instead of hiring one each day.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Self-hosted agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A *self-hosted agent* is an agent that you set up to run jobs and manage yourself. You can use self-hosted agents in Azure Pipelines or Azure DevOps Server.

notes.front: What are Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents?
notes.back: Self-hosted agents that run on an Azure virtual machine scale set and are autoscaled to meet demand.
notes.explanation: The elasticity means you need not run dedicated agents all the time.
notes.example: Like a staffing agency for build machines: more arrive when the queue grows, and they leave when it empties.
introduces: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents”, “Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents, hereafter referred to as scale set agents, are a form of self-hosted agents that can be autoscaled to meet your demands. This elasticity reduces your need to run dedicated agents all the time.
uses: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents

notes.front: What is Managed DevOps Pools?
notes.back: A fully managed service for creating Azure DevOps agent pools tailored to a team, with the machines in a Microsoft subscription.
notes.explanation: It is an evolution of scale set agent pools that simplifies creating custom pools.
notes.example: Like scale set agents, but Microsoft runs the scale set, not your subscription.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Managed DevOps Pools agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Managed DevOps Pools is an evolution of Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets agent pools. It simplifies custom pool creation even further by improving the scalability and reliability of custom pools. Managed DevOps Pools is a fully managed service. The virtual machines or containers that power agents live in a Microsoft Azure subscription and not in your own Azure subscription
uses: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents

notes.front: In Azure DevOps Services, what is a parallel job?
notes.back: A unit of compute capacity to run one pipeline job at a time; five parallel jobs let five pipeline jobs run at once.
notes.explanation: Jobs beyond the number of parallel jobs wait their turn.
notes.example: Like lanes in a swimming pool: one lane, one swimmer at a time; the rest queue.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure and pay for parallel jobs”, “What is a parallel job?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A parallel job in Azure DevOps Services represents the compute capacity to run a pipeline job. If you have one parallel job, you can run one pipeline job at a time. If you have five parallel jobs, you can run five pipeline jobs at a time.

notes.front: What is a GitHub-hosted runner?
notes.back: A GitHub-provided virtual machine, with the runner application and tools preinstalled, that runs GitHub Actions jobs.
notes.explanation: Machine maintenance and upgrades are handled for you.
notes.example: Like a Microsoft-hosted agent, but for GitHub Actions workflows.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub-hosted runners”, “Overview of GitHub-hosted runners”
notes.evidence: Each runner comes with the runner application and other tools preinstalled. {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom %}-hosted runners are available with Ubuntu Linux, Windows, or macOS operating systems. When you use a {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom %}-hosted runner, machine maintenance and upgrades are taken care of for you.

notes.front: What are GitHub-hosted runner images?
notes.back: The virtual machine images GitHub maintains for its standard hosted runners, listed with their tools in the `actions/runner-images` repository.
notes.explanation: The same repository holds announcements of major software updates on runners.
notes.example: Like the standard laptop set-up a company gives every new starter, published with its software list.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub-hosted runners”, “Runner images”
notes.evidence: maintains our own set of VM images for our standard hosted runners. The list of images and their included tools are managed in the [`actions/runner-images`](https://github.com/actions/runner-images) repository.

notes.front: What is a self-hosted runner?
notes.back: A system you deploy and manage yourself to run GitHub Actions jobs.
notes.explanation: You host the runner and customise the environment its jobs run in.
notes.example: Like a self-hosted agent in Azure Pipelines, but it takes jobs from GitHub Actions workflows.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Self-hosted runners”, “Self-hosted runners”
notes.evidence: A self-hosted runner is a system that you deploy and manage to execute jobs from {% data variables.product.prodname_actions %} on {% data variables.product.github %}.

notes.front: What is a larger runner in GitHub Actions?
notes.back: A GitHub-managed hosted runner with more resources than the standard ones, plus features such as static addresses and autoscaling.
notes.explanation: GitHub hosts them, with the runner application and tools preinstalled.
notes.example: Like a standard GitHub-hosted runner upgraded to a bigger machine with extra network options.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About larger runners” (github/docs on GitHub, data/reusables/actions/about-larger-runners.md)
notes.evidence: s are managed virtual machines with more resources than standard {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom %}-hosted runners. They offer the following advanced features: * More RAM, CPU, and disk space * Static IP addresses

notes.front: What is GitHub App authentication for Azure Pipelines?
notes.back: Connecting Azure Pipelines to GitHub through the installed Azure Pipelines GitHub App, so pipelines run under the Azure Pipelines identity.
notes.explanation: It is the recommended authentication type for continuous integration pipelines.
notes.example: Like giving a delivery firm its own staff badge instead of lending it your personal keys.
introduces: GitHub App authentication for Azure Pipelines
notes.source: Microsoft, “Build GitHub repositories”, “GitHub app authentication” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Azure Pipelines GitHub App is the **recommended** authentication type for continuous integration pipelines. After you install the GitHub App in your GitHub account or organization, your pipeline will run without using your personal GitHub identity.
uses: GitHub App authentication for Azure Pipelines

notes.front: Which kind of Azure Pipelines pipeline does Microsoft recommend if you are new to Azure Pipelines?
notes.back: `YAML` pipelines.
notes.explanation: Existing Classic pipelines can keep running or be migrated to `YAML`.
notes.source: Microsoft, “YAML vs Classic Pipelines”, “YAML vs Classic Pipelines” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you are new to Azure Pipelines, it is recommended to start with YAML pipelines. For existing Classic pipelines, you can choose to continue using them or migrate to YAML pipelines.

notes.front: Where is a `YAML` pipeline’s definition kept, and how can branches differ?
notes.back: In `azure-pipelines.yml`, versioned with the application code; each branch can customise the pipeline by editing its copy.
notes.explanation: The file follows the same branching structure as the code it builds.
notes.source: Microsoft, “YAML vs Classic Pipelines”, “Define pipelines using YAML” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Your pipeline configuration resides in a YAML file named `azure-pipelines.yml`, alongside your application. - The YAML file is versioned alongside your application code, adhering to the same branching structure. - Each branch can customize the pipeline by editing the `azure-pipelines.yml` file.

notes.front: In which kind of Azure Pipelines pipeline are deployment gates available?
notes.back: Only in Classic release pipelines, not in `YAML` or Classic build pipelines.
notes.explanation: The feature table marks Gates as unavailable for `YAML` and Classic Pipeline, and available for Classic Release.
notes.source: Microsoft, “YAML vs Classic Pipelines”, “Feature availability” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | **Gates** | Automate release controls by evaluating health signals from external services before completing a deployment. | :::image type="icon" source="../../media/icons/delete-icon.png" border="false"::: | :::image type="icon" source="../../media/icons/delete-icon.png" border="false"::: |

notes.front: A team wants pipeline changes reviewed in pull requests alongside the code, and a feature branch able to change its own build steps. Which pipeline type fits?
notes.choices:
A) Classic build pipeline
B) Classic release pipeline
C) A task group
D) `YAML` pipeline
notes.back: D) `YAML` pipeline
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are edited in the web portal, outside version control. C is a Classic building block, not a pipeline type.
notes.explanation: A `YAML` pipeline file is versioned with the code, and each branch can customise it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “YAML vs Classic Pipelines”, “Define pipelines using YAML” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Each branch can customize the pipeline by editing the `azure-pipelines.yml` file. - Keeping the pipeline configuration in version control ensures that any changes that cause issues or unexpected outcomes can be easily identified within your codebase.

notes.front: How is the GitHub-hosted runner application related to the Azure Pipelines agent?
notes.back: It is a fork of the Azure Pipelines agent.
notes.explanation: GitHub runs its Linux and Windows runners on virtual machines in Microsoft Azure.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub-hosted runners”, “Cloud hosts used by GitHub-hosted runners”
notes.evidence: hosts Linux and Windows runners on virtual machines in Microsoft Azure with the {% data variables.product.prodname_actions %} runner application installed. The {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom %}-hosted runner application is a fork of the Azure Pipelines Agent.

notes.front: A company runs its builds on its own machines. In Azure Pipelines it pays for self-hosted parallel jobs beyond the free tier. If it moves those builds to GitHub Actions on self-hosted runners, what does GitHub charge for the runner usage?
notes.choices:
A) Per registered runner
B) Per minute, like larger runners
C) Nothing: GitHub Actions usage is free for self-hosted runners
D) Per parallel job, as in Azure Pipelines
notes.back: C) Nothing: GitHub Actions usage is free for self-hosted runners
notes.choicesExplained: B is how larger runners are billed. A and D are wrong: GitHub charges nothing for self-hosted runner usage, and paying per parallel job is the Azure Pipelines model.
notes.explanation: GitHub Actions usage is free on self-hosted runners; the company still pays to maintain the machines.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Actions billing”, “How use of GitHub Actions is measured”
notes.evidence: usage is **free** for **self-hosted runners** and for **public repositories** that use standard {% data variables.product.github %}-hosted runners.

notes.front: Can you use Microsoft-hosted agents with an on-premises Azure DevOps Server?
notes.back: No. They are available only in Azure DevOps Services; with Azure DevOps Server you must use self-hosted agents.
notes.explanation: The Azure Pipelines agent pool is not available on-premises either.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines”, “Microsoft-hosted agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Microsoft-hosted agents are only available with Azure DevOps Services, which is hosted in the cloud. You can't use Microsoft-hosted agents or the Azure Pipelines agent pool with on-premises Azure DevOps Server. With these on-premises versions, you must use self-hosted agents.

notes.front: A bank runs Azure DevOps Server in its own data centre. Which agent type can its pipelines use?
notes.choices:
A) Self-hosted agents
B) GitHub-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines
C) Managed DevOps Pools
D) Microsoft-hosted agents
notes.back: A) Self-hosted agents
notes.choicesExplained: D, B and C are listed for Azure DevOps Services only.
notes.explanation: Self-hosted agents are the one type available in both Azure DevOps Services and Azure DevOps Server.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Azure Pipelines agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | [Self-hosted agents](#install) | Agents that you configure and manage that are hosted on your virtual machines (VMs). | Azure DevOps Services, Azure DevOps Server |

notes.front: Which side starts communication between a self-hosted agent and Azure Pipelines?
notes.back: Always the agent: it pulls jobs over `HTTP` or `HTTPS`, listening to the job queue with a long poll.
notes.explanation: This pull model lets you place the agent in different network topologies.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Communication with Azure Pipelines” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The agent always initiates this communication. All the messages from the agent to Azure Pipelines or Azure DevOps Server happen over HTTP or HTTPS, depending on how you configure the agent. This pull model allows you to configure the agent to different topologies

notes.front: Which role do you need to register an agent in an agent pool, and is it kept on the agent afterwards?
notes.back: Agent pool administrator; it is needed only at registration and is not persisted on the agent.
notes.explanation: After registration the agent uses a listener token to watch the job queue.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Communication with Azure Pipelines” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The **Agent pool administrator** role is needed only at the time of registration and isn't persisted on the agent.

notes.front: A pipeline must deploy to servers in an on-premises data centre that Microsoft-hosted agents cannot reach through the firewall. What does the documentation advise?
notes.choices:
A) Open the firewall to every Azure address range
B) Configure self-hosted agents on on-premises computers that can reach the targets and the internet
C) Use a larger runner
D) Use GitHub-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines
notes.back: B) Configure self-hosted agents on on-premises computers that can reach the targets and the internet
notes.choicesExplained: A exposes far more than needed. C is a GitHub Actions runner, not an Azure Pipelines agent. D is still hosted outside the data centre.
notes.explanation: Deploying agents need line-of-sight connectivity to their target servers.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Communication to deploy to target servers” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If your on-premises environments don't have connectivity to a Microsoft-hosted agent pool, which is typically the case due to intermediate firewalls, you need to manually configure self-hosted agents on on-premises computers. The agents must have connectivity to the target on-premises environments, and access to the internet to connect to Azure Pipelines or Azure DevOps Server.

notes.front: What is the difference between system capabilities and user capabilities on a self-hosted agent?
notes.back: System capabilities are discovered by the agent software; user capabilities are ones you define.
notes.explanation: System capabilities include the machine name, operating system and installed software versions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Capabilities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Every self-hosted agent has a set of capabilities that indicate what it can do. Capabilities are name/value pairs that are either: * Capabilities that the agent software discovers, called *system capabilities*. * Capabilities that you define, called *user capabilities*.

notes.front: How do demands in a pipeline decide which agent runs a job?
notes.back: The job is sent only to agents whose capabilities match the demands.
notes.explanation: Demands are added in `YAML` with a `demands:` line in the `pool` section.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Capabilities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you author a pipeline, you specify certain *demands* of the agent. The system sends the job only to agents that have capabilities that match the demands specified in the pipeline. As a result, agent capabilities allow you to direct jobs to specific agents.

notes.front: Do you need demands and capabilities to target a Microsoft-hosted agent?
notes.back: No. With Microsoft-hosted agents you select an image that matches the job’s needs.
notes.explanation: Demands and capabilities are designed for self-hosted agents.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Capabilities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Demands and capabilities are designed for use with self-hosted agents so that jobs can be matched with an agent that meets the requirements of the job. When you use Microsoft-hosted agents, you select an image for the agent that matches the requirements of the job.

notes.front: Only two self-hosted agents in the Default pool have a licensed document-rendering toolkit installed, recorded as a user capability `PdfKit`. How do you make a `YAML` job run only on them?
notes.choices:
A) Set `vmImage: PdfKit`
B) Add a build tag `PdfKit`
C) Buy another parallel job
D) Add `demands: PdfKit` to the job’s `pool` section
notes.back: D) Add `demands: PdfKit` to the job’s `pool` section
notes.choicesExplained: A picks a Microsoft-hosted image, not a self-hosted capability. B labels runs after the fact. C adds capacity but does not steer the job.
notes.explanation: A demand with an exists check sends the job only to agents that have that capability.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Configure demands” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To add a demand to your YAML build pipeline, add the `demands:` line to the `pool` section.

notes.front: What machine do you get for each job on Microsoft-hosted agents?
notes.back: A freshly imaged agent for each job.
notes.explanation: The virtual machines are reimaged after each run, and each hosts a single agent.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines”, “Capabilities and limitations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You get a freshly imaged agent for each job in your pipeline.

notes.front: A team on Microsoft-hosted agents notices that files downloaded in one job’s run are never there when the next job starts. Why?
notes.choices:
A) The demands do not match
B) The agent pool is misconfigured
C) The organisation has only one parallel job
D) Each job gets a freshly imaged agent
notes.back: D) Each job gets a freshly imaged agent
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and A would not remove files: a single parallel job only queues jobs, and demands only choose agents.
notes.explanation: Machine-level state does not carry over on Microsoft-hosted agents; it does on self-hosted agents.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines”, “Security” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Microsoft-hosted agents are run in individual VMs, which are reimaged after each run. Each agent is dedicated to a single organization, and each VM hosts only a single agent.

notes.front: In a `YAML` pipeline with no pool specified, which agent pool and image are used?
notes.back: The Azure Pipelines agent pool, with the `ubuntu-latest` image.
notes.explanation: To choose another image, set `vmImage` on its own line under `pool`, for example `vmImage: 'windows-latest'`.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines”, “Software” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The `ubuntu-latest` image is the default image for YAML pipelines if no image is specified.

notes.front: How do you ask for software to be added to the Microsoft-hosted agent images?
notes.back: Open an issue on the `actions/runner-images` repository, not a support ticket.
notes.explanation: That repository holds the scripts that generate the images.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines”, “Software” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To request software to be added to Microsoft-hosted agents, don't create a feedback request on this document or open a support ticket. Instead, open an issue on our repository, where we manage the scripts to generate various images.

notes.front: What can you do if Microsoft-hosted agents are not powerful enough or lack disk space?
notes.back: Microsoft will not enlarge them; use self-hosted agents, scale set agents or Managed DevOps Pools.
notes.explanation: Microsoft cannot honour requests for more disk space or more powerful machines.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines”, “Hardware” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: We can't honor requests to increase disk space on Microsoft-hosted agents, or to provision more powerful machines. If the specifications of Microsoft-hosted agents do not meet your needs, then you should consider self-hosted agents or scale set agents or Managed DevOps Pools.

notes.front: How much storage do Microsoft-hosted agents give for your source and build outputs?
notes.back: 10 gigabytes.
notes.explanation: The space is used up by checking out code, downloading packages, pulling images and writing intermediate files.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines”, “Capabilities and limitations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Provide 10 GB of storage for your source and build outputs.

notes.front: What are two things Microsoft-hosted agents do not offer?
notes.back: Any two of: remote connection; joining your corporate network; bigger machines; preloaded custom software; rolling back to an earlier image.
notes.explanation: Software can still be installed during a run, for example with tool installer tasks.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines”, “Capabilities and limitations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Microsoft-hosted agents do not offer: * The ability to remotely connect. * The ability to drop artifacts to a UNC file share. * The ability to join machines directly to your corporate network. * The ability to get bigger or more powerful build machines. * The ability to preload custom software.

notes.front: A build needs a licensed compiler that takes an hour to install, 40 gigabytes of free disk and a machine joined to the corporate domain. Which option meets all three?
notes.choices:
A) A self-hosted agent on a machine you prepare
B) A paid Microsoft-hosted parallel job
C) A bigger Microsoft-hosted image on request
D) Microsoft-hosted agents with a tool installer task
notes.back: A) A self-hosted agent on a machine you prepare
notes.choicesExplained: D still installs the compiler every run and cannot join the domain. B lifts time limits, not disk or network limits. C is not offered: Microsoft will not provide bigger machines.
notes.explanation: Self-hosted agents let you install the software you need, and their machine state persists between runs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Self-hosted agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Self-hosted agents give you more control to install dependent software that you need for your builds and deployments. Also, machine-level caches and configuration persist from run to run, which can boost speed.

notes.front: How do you let Microsoft-hosted agents through a firewall to your resources?
notes.back: Allow the published address ranges for every region in your organisation’s Azure geography; service tags cannot be used.
notes.explanation: An agent can run in any region mapped to your geography, and the ranges change over time.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines”, “Service tags” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Microsoft-hosted agents can't be listed by service tags. If you're trying to grant hosted agents access to your resources, you'll need to follow the IP range allow listing method.

notes.front: How are GitHub-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines billed, compared with Microsoft-hosted agents?
notes.back: Per minute of use, while Microsoft-hosted agents use a concurrency-based pool.
notes.explanation: GitHub-hosted agents also offer more powerful machine configurations.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “GitHub-hosted agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Unlike the Microsoft-hosted agents that use a concurrency-based pool, GitHub-hosted agents bill per minute of usage and offer more powerful machine configurations.

notes.front: How many self-hosted agents does Microsoft recommend installing on one machine?
notes.back: Only one.
notes.explanation: Two or more agents on a machine might hurt performance and pipeline results.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Self-hosted agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Although multiple agents can be installed per machine, we strongly recommend that you install only one agent per machine. When you install two or more agents, it might adversely affect performance and the result of your pipelines.

notes.front: When is it useful to run a self-hosted Azure Pipelines agent inside a Docker container?
notes.back: When you want agents run by an outer orchestrator, such as Azure Container Instances.
notes.explanation: The agent runs in a Windows Server Core container on Windows hosts or an Ubuntu container on Linux hosts.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Run a self-hosted agent in Docker”, “Run a self-hosted agent in Docker” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can set up a self-hosted agent in Azure Pipelines to run inside a Windows Server Core (for Windows hosts), or Ubuntu container (for Linux hosts) with Docker. This is useful when you want to run agents with outer orchestration, such as Azure Container Instances.

notes.front: What do scale set agents give you that Microsoft-hosted agents do not?
notes.back: Flexibility over the size and the image of the machines the agents run on.
notes.explanation: They suit teams that like Microsoft-hosted agents but are limited by what those offer.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents”, “Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Unlike Microsoft-hosted agents, you have flexibility over the size and the image of machines on which agents run. If you like Microsoft-hosted agents but are limited by what they offer, you should consider scale set agents.
uses: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents

notes.front: Which operating systems can scale set agents run?
notes.back: Windows or Linux only; not macOS.
notes.explanation: Mac agents cannot run on scale sets.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents”, “Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You cannot run Mac agents using scale sets. You can only run Windows or Linux agents this way.
uses: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents

notes.front: In a scale set agent pool, what happens if you set Number of agents to keep on standby to 0?
notes.back: Azure Pipelines starts a virtual machine only when it has a job.
notes.explanation: The setting can conserve cost for a low volume of jobs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents”, “Create the scale set agent pool” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you set **Number of agents to keep on standby** to **0**, for example to conserve cost for a low volume of jobs, Azure Pipelines will start a VM only when it has a job.
uses: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents

notes.front: A team builds untrusted contributions on its own machines and wants every job to start on a clean machine, while keeping its own image. Which option fits?
notes.choices:
A) Scale set agents with Automatically tear down virtual machines after every use
B) One self-hosted agent that runs every job
C) Several agents on one machine
D) A user capability named `clean`
notes.back: A) Scale set agents with Automatically tear down virtual machines after every use
notes.choicesExplained: B keeps state between jobs. C is discouraged and still shares a machine. D is a label; it cleans nothing.
notes.explanation: With that setting the virtual machine goes offline after a job and is reimaged before taking another.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents”, “Create the scale set agent pool” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Automatically tear down virtual machines after every use** - The VM goes offline after running a job and is reimaged before picking up another job.
uses: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents

notes.front: When you build a custom image for scale set agents, should you install the Azure Pipelines agent in it?
notes.back: No. Azure Pipelines installs the agent automatically as it provisions each new virtual machine.
notes.explanation: The image can be any Linux or Windows image, from Azure Marketplace or your own.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents”, “Create the scale set” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Select any Linux or Windows image - either from Azure Marketplace or your own custom image - to create the scale set. Don't pre-install Azure Pipelines agent in the image. Azure Pipelines automatically installs the agent as it provisions new virtual machines.
uses: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents

notes.front: Can you use the Microsoft-hosted agent images directly for your scale set agents?
notes.back: No, licensing prevents Microsoft distributing them, but the scripts that generate them are open source for building your own.
notes.explanation: The scripts live in the `actions/runner-images` repository.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents”, “Create the scale set” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Licensing considerations limit us from distributing Microsoft-hosted images. We are unable to provide these images for you to use in your scale set agents. But, the scripts that we use to generate these images are open source. You are free to use these scripts and create your own custom images.
uses: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents

notes.front: A team wants autoscaling agents that start with its own toolchain and a 256-gigabyte disk, built as a reusable virtual machine template. What is the documented approach?
notes.choices:
A) Ask Microsoft for a bigger hosted image
B) Install the Azure Pipelines agent in the image first
C) Use the Microsoft-hosted images in the scale set
D) Create a virtual machine with the tools and disk size, capture it as a custom image, and create the scale set from it
notes.back: D) Create a virtual machine with the tools and disk size, capture it as a custom image, and create the scale set from it
notes.choicesExplained: A is not offered. B is advised against: Azure Pipelines installs the agent itself. C is impossible: those images are not distributed.
notes.explanation: The documented steps begin by creating a virtual machine with the operating system image and the disk size you want.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents”, “Create a scale set with custom image, software, or disk size” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Create a VM with your desired OS image and optionally expand the OS disk size from 128 GB to `<myDiskSizeGb>`.
uses: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents

notes.front: When a scale set agent machine is created, what runs first, and what happens if it fails?
notes.back: The Custom Script Extension runs before the Azure Pipelines agent extension; a non-zero exit code aborts and deletes the virtual machine.
notes.explanation: The agent extension then downloads the latest agent and registers it in the pool.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents”, “Lifecycle of a Scale Set Agent” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If the Custom Script Extension is installed, it's executed before the Azure Pipelines Agent extension. If the Custom Script Extension returns a non-zero exit code, the VM creation process is aborted and will be deleted.
uses: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents

notes.front: If you are considering autoscalable, self-hosted agent pools, what does Microsoft recommend you consider?
notes.back: Managed DevOps Pools.
notes.explanation: It is the evolution of scale set agent pools.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Azure Pipelines agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you're considering using autoscalable, self-hosted agent pools, we recommend that you consider Managed DevOps Pools.

notes.front: A platform team wants custom, autoscaling agent pools but does not want the agent virtual machines in its own Azure subscription. Which option fits?
notes.choices:
A) Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents
B) Managed DevOps Pools
C) Self-hosted agents on its own servers
D) Agents in Docker on its own hosts
notes.back: B) Managed DevOps Pools
notes.choicesExplained: A runs the scale set in your subscription. C and D run on machines you own.
notes.explanation: The machines behind Managed DevOps Pools live in a Microsoft Azure subscription, not yours.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Azure Pipelines agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | [Managed DevOps Pools agents](#managed-devops-pools-agents) | Managed DevOps Pools is a fully managed service. Virtual machines or containers that power the agents live in a Microsoft Azure subscription and not in your own Azure subscription. | Azure DevOps Services |
uses: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents

notes.front: At which levels of a `YAML` file can you specify the pool?
notes.back: At pipeline, stage and job level.
notes.explanation: So one job can use Microsoft-hosted agents while another uses a self-hosted pool.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines”, “Use a Microsoft-hosted agent” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The specification of a pool can be done at multiple levels in a YAML file. > If you notice that your pipeline isn't running on the expected image, make sure that you verify the pool specification at the pipeline, stage, and job levels.

notes.front: A pipeline should build on Microsoft-hosted agents but deploy from an agent inside the corporate network. How do you set this up?
notes.choices:
A) Use one pool for the whole pipeline
B) Give each job its own `pool`: the build job uses `vmImage`, the deploy job names the self-hosted pool
C) Put all agents in the Azure Pipelines pool
D) Run both jobs on a larger runner
notes.back: B) Give each job its own `pool`: the build job uses `vmImage`, the deploy job names the self-hosted pool
notes.choicesExplained: A forces both jobs onto the same kind of agent. C is wrong: that pool is Microsoft’s hosted pool. D is a GitHub Actions runner.
notes.explanation: Pools can be set per job, so a pipeline can mix hosted and self-hosted agents.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines”, “Use a Microsoft-hosted agent” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The specification of a pool can be done at multiple levels in a YAML file.

notes.front: What does the Microsoft-hosted free tier give a private project in Azure DevOps Services?
notes.back: One parallel job running up to 60 minutes at a time, up to 1,800 minutes (30 hours) a month.
notes.explanation: Unlike the self-hosted free tier, it is not granted automatically; you must enable it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure and pay for parallel jobs”, “What is a parallel job?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you enable the free tier, for **private projects** you get one free job that runs for up to 60 minutes each time, with a monthly limit of 1,800 minutes (30 hours).

notes.front: How do you enable the Microsoft-hosted free tier of parallel jobs?
notes.back: Link the Azure DevOps organisation to a valid Azure subscription by setting up billing.
notes.explanation: Once billing is configured, the free grant applies automatically to private projects.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure and pay for parallel jobs”, “How do I enable the free tier of parallel jobs?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To receive the free grant of parallel jobs, link your Azure DevOps organization to a valid Azure subscription. Set up billing for your organization to link an Azure subscription. Once you configure billing, the free grant automatically applies to private projects in the organization.

notes.front: How long can a job run on a paid Microsoft-hosted parallel job?
notes.back: Up to 360 minutes (6 hours), with no monthly time limit.
notes.explanation: Paying removes the free tier’s 60-minute and monthly limits.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines”, “Capabilities and limitations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Paid parallel jobs remove the monthly time limit and allow you to run each job for up to 360 minutes (6 hours).

notes.front: On the free tier, you buy your first Microsoft-hosted parallel job. How many jobs can now run at once?
notes.back: Still one: the first purchase only removes the time limits. Two concurrent jobs need two purchased parallel jobs.
notes.explanation: The purchase replaces the free job rather than adding a second.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure and pay for parallel jobs”, “What is a parallel job?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you purchase your first Microsoft-hosted parallel job, the number of parallel jobs you have in the organization is still one. To run two jobs concurrently, you need to purchase two parallel jobs if you're currently on the free tier. The first purchase only removes the time limits on the first job.

notes.front: On the Microsoft-hosted free tier, a private project’s 80-minute integration test job keeps being cut off. Which change lets it finish?
notes.choices:
A) Add a second self-hosted agent
B) Rename the pipeline’s run number format
C) Buy a Microsoft-hosted parallel job, or split the work into shorter jobs
D) Add demands to the job
notes.back: C) Buy a Microsoft-hosted parallel job, or split the work into shorter jobs
notes.choicesExplained: A does not change the hosted time limit. B only renames runs. D only chooses agents.
notes.explanation: Free-tier jobs run up to 60 minutes; a paid job runs up to 360, and splitting the pipeline into jobs is the documented tip.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure and pay for parallel jobs”, “What is a parallel job?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If your pipeline exceeds the maximum job time limit, try splitting your pipeline > into multiple jobs.

notes.front: For self-hosted parallel jobs in Azure DevOps Services, what are you charged for?
notes.back: The number of jobs you want to run at the same time, not the number of agents registered.
notes.explanation: You can register any number of self-hosted agents, and self-hosted jobs have no time limits.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure and pay for parallel jobs”, “What is a parallel job?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For self-hosted parallel jobs, you can register any number of self-hosted agents in your organization. We charge based on the number of jobs you want to run at a time, not the number of agents registered. There are no time limits on self-hosted jobs.

notes.front: What does the self-hosted free tier include for private projects?
notes.back: One parallel job, plus one more for each active Visual Studio Enterprise subscriber in the organisation.
notes.explanation: The self-hosted free tier is granted automatically.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure and pay for parallel jobs”, “What is a parallel job?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For private projects, the free tier includes one parallel job plus one parallel job for each active Visual Studio Enterprise subscriber who is a member of your organization.

notes.front: What rule of thumb does Microsoft give for how many parallel jobs an organisation needs?
notes.back: About one parallel job for every four to five users.
notes.explanation: More may be needed for several teams, branches or applications building at once.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure and pay for parallel jobs”, “How many parallel jobs do I need?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A simple rule of thumb: Estimate that you need one parallel job for every four to five users in your organization.

notes.front: An organisation with one parallel job starts three pipelines at 09:00. What happens?
notes.choices:
A) All three run at once
B) One runs; the other two queue until a parallel job is free
C) Two are cancelled
D) Azure DevOps buys more parallel jobs automatically
notes.back: B) One runs; the other two queue until a parallel job is free
notes.choicesExplained: A needs three parallel jobs. C is wrong: extra jobs wait rather than fail. D is wrong: you buy more yourself in Organization settings.
notes.explanation: Concurrent jobs beyond the number of parallel jobs are queued until one finishes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Pipelines agents”, “Parallel jobs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If your organization has a single parallel job, you can run a single job at a time in your organization. Any other concurrent jobs are queued until the first job finishes.

notes.front: What happens to a workflow run queued for a GitHub-hosted runner that is not picked up within 45 minutes?
notes.back: It is discarded.
notes.explanation: This applies once the run has been successfully queued.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub-hosted runners”, “Workflow continuity”
notes.evidence: if the workflow run has been successfully queued, but has not been processed by a {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom %}-hosted runner within 45 minutes, then the queued workflow run is discarded.

notes.front: How often is the software in GitHub-owned runner images updated, and how do you see what a run used?
notes.back: Weekly; the workflow log’s Set up job, Runner Image section links to the included software.
notes.explanation: The update takes several days, so the published list changes only after the whole deployment ends.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub-hosted runners”, “Preinstalled software for GitHub-owned images”
notes.evidence: The software tools included in our GitHub-owned images are updated weekly. The update process takes several days, and the list of preinstalled software on the `main` branch is updated after the whole deployment ends.

notes.front: With a self-hosted runner, who updates the operating system and other software?
notes.back: You do; GitHub updates only the self-hosted runner application, and you may turn that off.
notes.explanation: Self-hosted runners give more control of hardware, operating system and tools than GitHub-hosted runners.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Self-hosted runners”, “Self-hosted runners”
notes.evidence: * Receive automatic updates for the self-hosted runner application only, though you may disable automatic updates of the runner.

notes.front: How does a self-hosted runner differ from a GitHub-hosted runner in who looks after the machine and whether jobs start clean?
notes.back: Self-hosted: you maintain it, and jobs need not start on a clean instance. GitHub-hosted: GitHub handles maintenance and upgrades.
notes.explanation: Because a self-hosted runner need not start clean, files left by one job can still be there when the next job starts.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Self-hosted runners”, “Self-hosted runners”
notes.evidence: * Don't need to have a clean instance for every job execution.

notes.front: How do repository-level and organisation-level self-hosted runners differ?
notes.back: Repository-level runners serve one repository; organisation-level runners can process jobs for many repositories in the organisation.
notes.explanation: Organisation owners choose which repositories may create repository-level runners.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Self-hosted runners”, “Self-hosted runners”
notes.evidence: Repository-level runners are dedicated to a single repository, while organization-level runners can process jobs for multiple repositories in an organization.

notes.front: A workflow must reach a licence server on the office network and use a special hardware test rig in the building. Which runner fits?
notes.choices:
A) A standard GitHub-hosted runner
B) A self-hosted runner in the office
C) A larger runner with more memory
D) A GitHub-hosted runner with a custom image
notes.back: B) A self-hosted runner in the office
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D run on GitHub’s infrastructure, away from the office rig; more memory or a custom image does not bring the hardware closer.
notes.explanation: Self-hosted runners can use machines your company already maintains, on-premises or in a cloud.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Self-hosted runners”, “Self-hosted runners”
notes.evidence: Allow you to use machines and services that your company already maintains and pays to use.

notes.front: Do larger runners use the included free minutes on private repositories?
notes.back: No. Larger runners are always billed at the per-minute rate, for private and public repositories.
notes.explanation: You pay only for the time workflows run on them, not for idle larger runners.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Larger runners”, “Billing”
notes.evidence: s are not eligible for the use of included minutes on private repositories. For both private and public repositories, when {% data variables.actions.hosted_runners %} are in use, they will always be billed at the per-minute rate.

notes.front: A company’s firewall allows only a fixed list of source addresses, and its GitHub Actions jobs need more memory than standard hosted runners. Which GitHub-hosted option fits?
notes.choices:
A) Standard GitHub-hosted runners
B) GitHub-hosted runner images
C) A larger runner with static IP addresses
D) Microsoft-hosted agents
notes.back: C) A larger runner with static IP addresses
notes.choicesExplained: A lacks both the extra memory and fixed addresses. B is a list of images, not a runner type. D is an Azure Pipelines agent, not a GitHub Actions runner.
notes.explanation: Static addresses let you configure firewall allowlists, and larger runners have more resources.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Larger runners”, “What you can do with larger runners”
notes.evidence: * **Static IP addresses**: Assign static IP addresses from a specific range to runners, allowing you to configure firewall allowlists.

notes.front: For which usage is GitHub Actions free?
notes.back: Self-hosted runners, and public repositories using standard GitHub-hosted runners.
notes.explanation: Private repositories get a plan-based quota of minutes and storage for GitHub-hosted runners.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Actions billing”, “How use of GitHub Actions is measured”
notes.evidence: usage is **free** for **self-hosted runners** and for **public repositories** that use standard {% data variables.product.github %}-hosted runners.

notes.front: Who is charged for GitHub Actions minutes used on a private repository?
notes.back: The repository owner, not the person who triggered the run.
notes.explanation: Anyone with write access can run actions, and the costs go to the owner.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Actions billing”, “How use of GitHub Actions is measured”
notes.evidence: Minutes usage is charged to the repository owner, not the person who triggered the workflow runs.

notes.front: Which GitHub storage shares one pooled allowance with Actions artifacts, and which has its own?
notes.back: GitHub Packages shares the pool with artifacts; the Actions cache has a separate 10-gigabyte allowance per repository.
notes.explanation: Storage is billed on an hourly accrual through the month.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Actions billing”, “How storage billing works”
notes.evidence: * **Cache storage:** Actions cache storage is a separate allowance of 10 GB per repository. Cache storage is not shared with artifacts or {% data variables.product.prodname_registry %}.

notes.front: A contractor with write access triggers many long GitHub Actions runs on a company’s private repository using GitHub-hosted runners. Whose minutes are used?
notes.choices:
A) The contractor’s personal account
B) Nobody’s: private repositories are free
C) GitHub’s free public pool
D) The repository owner’s account
notes.back: D) The repository owner’s account
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: usage is not charged to the person who triggers runs. B is wrong: private repositories draw on a plan quota, then billing. C applies to public repositories on standard runners.
notes.explanation: Minutes are charged to the repository owner.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Actions billing”, “How use of GitHub Actions is measured”
notes.evidence: Anyone with write access to a repository can run actions. Any costs of running the actions are billed to the repository owner.

notes.front: Of the three ways Azure Pipelines authenticates to GitHub, which runs under the Azure Pipelines identity and works with GitHub Checks?
notes.back: The GitHub App; OAuth and personal access tokens use your personal GitHub identity and do not work with Checks.
notes.explanation: With the app, builds and status updates use the Azure Pipelines identity.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Build GitHub repositories”, “Access to GitHub repositories” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | 1. GitHub App | The Azure Pipelines identity  | Yes | | 2. OAuth           | Your personal GitHub identity | No  | | 3. Personal access token (PAT) | Your personal GitHub identity | No  |
uses: GitHub App authentication for Azure Pipelines

notes.front: Who can install the Azure Pipelines GitHub App?
notes.back: A GitHub organisation owner or a repository admin.
notes.explanation: Without the right GitHub permissions, the repository does not appear when you create the pipeline.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Build GitHub repositories”, “Permissions needed in GitHub” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Installation of Azure Pipelines GitHub app requires you to be a GitHub organization owner or repository admin.
uses: GitHub App authentication for Azure Pipelines

notes.front: What is the risk of installing the Azure Pipelines GitHub App for all repositories in an organisation?
notes.back: Its token can reach every repository, including private ones.
notes.explanation: For security, Microsoft recommends keeping private and public repositories in separate organisations.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Build GitHub repositories”, “GitHub app authentication” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: However, if the app is installed for all repositories, the token used by the application will have access to all repositories, including private ones. For security reasons, it is recommended to separate private and public repositories at the organization level.
uses: GitHub App authentication for Azure Pipelines

notes.front: A lead developer leaves the company, and every Azure Pipelines build of the team’s GitHub repositories stops, because they authenticated with his personal token. Which set-up avoids this?
notes.choices:
A) Another developer’s OAuth connection
B) A new personal access token from a colleague
C) A Classic pipeline
D) The Azure Pipelines GitHub App installed in the organisation
notes.back: D) The Azure Pipelines GitHub App installed in the organisation
notes.choicesExplained: A and B still depend on one person’s GitHub identity staying active. C changes the editor, not the authentication.
notes.explanation: With the app, pipelines run without using any personal GitHub identity.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Build GitHub repositories”, “Personal access token (PAT) authentication” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Builds and GitHub status updates will be performed on behalf of your personal GitHub identity. For builds to keep working, your repository access must remain active.
uses: GitHub App authentication for Azure Pipelines

notes.front: In Azure DevOps, what state is the organisation-level control for pull requests from forked GitHub repositories in for existing organisations, and for organisations created from September 2023?
notes.back: Off for existing organisations; new organisations from September 2023 have Securely build pull requests from forked repositories turned on by default.
notes.explanation: The page ties the default to when the organisation was created: organisations that already existed keep the control off.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Build GitHub repositories”, “Contributions from forks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The control is off for existing organizations. Starting September 2023, new organizations have **Securely build pull requests from forked repositories** turned on by default

notes.front: Under the Securely build pull requests from forked repositories option, what three restrictions apply?
notes.back: No secrets for fork builds, no normal-build permissions, and builds must be triggered by a pull request comment.
notes.explanation: Projects can still choose not to build such pull requests at all.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Build GitHub repositories”, “Contributions from forks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you choose the **Securely build pull requests from forked repositories** option, all pipelines, organization or project-wide, *cannot* make secrets available to builds of PRs from forked repositories, *cannot* make these builds have the same permissions as normal builds, and *must* be triggered by a PR comment.

notes.front: By default, are a GitHub pipeline’s secrets available to pull request builds from forks?
notes.back: No. You must tick Make secrets available to builds of forks, which affects security.
notes.explanation: The secrets include the repository token, service connection credentials, secure files and secret variables.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Build GitHub repositories”, “Contributions from forks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By default with GitHub pipelines, secrets associated with your build pipeline aren’t made available to pull request builds of forks.

notes.front: A public open-source repository must build pull requests from forks. The team worries malicious code could compromise the build machine and steal secrets from other pipelines. What does Microsoft advise?
notes.choices:
A) Give fork builds the same permissions as regular builds
B) Build them on the self-hosted agent that also runs releases
C) Tick Make secrets available to builds of forks
D) Build fork pull requests on Microsoft-hosted agents, which are deleted after each build
notes.back: D) Build fork pull requests on Microsoft-hosted agents, which are deleted after each build
notes.choicesExplained: B puts untrusted code next to other pipelines’ secrets. C and A widen what a malicious pull request could reach.
notes.explanation: A compromised Microsoft-hosted machine leaves no lasting impact, because it is deleted after the build.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Build GitHub repositories”, “Important security considerations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use a Microsoft-hosted agent pool to build pull requests from forks. Microsoft-hosted agent machines are immediately deleted after they complete a build, so there’s no lasting impact if they're compromised.
